why: The spelling, vocabulary, and punctuation of the translation, revised by explicit editorial decisions. A word is respelled or modernized wherever the translation, its notes, and its front and back matter print it as a whole word; a word with a scope of scripture is revised only in numbered scripture and marked note lemmas (fq) and readings (fqa), wherever they stand. Book titles and metadata, headings, introduction paragraphs, and explanatory commentary are outside that scripture scope. The scope marks the archaisms, the King James inflections and past tenses carried into Brenton’s Scripture, which the notes’ commentary and the prefaces do not take; a modernization has no scope, and reaches them as it reaches the text. Numbered scripture in d paragraphs, including Psalm superscriptions, remains in scope. Plain quotation marks do not establish scope. Names are respelled first. Global spelling, vocabulary, article, possessive, and participle decisions affect source prose and run next, followed by a separate single sweep of scoped grammar decisions. The ligatures are written out last of all. A verse's change is made to the words of that verse alone, which must have them once, as the names leave them, and to the notes that quote them. A note's lemma retains the verse's internal punctuation, including a colon before the separate colon that introduces the note: Luke 4:41, Revelation 14:13, and Haggai 2:14 keep both. Luke 1:45 retains its local comma revision under luke-belief-clause; avoiding two colons alone does not require another verse revision. Verses' changes stand in groups, each group under the reason its changes share. Each gives its reason. An isolated alternative whose word is also a plural noun may name its stable source note as its exact context. Passage changes name a stable note key or a front/back-matter unit and the plain words met once there; only punctuation, associated spacing, and sentence-initial capitalization may change, with lowercase word initials also allowed in keyed notes. A phrase is revised as a word is; possessives and articles follow the immediately following sound, including an intervening adjective: my and thy before consonant sounds, mine and thine before vowel sounds and silent h; a before consonant sounds, an before vowel sounds and silent h. Independent mine and thine stay. Capitalization is decided separately. A word may except the phrases it must not change, which the edition must print. Words that a character style divides keep their division, and so does the lemma that quotes them at its note; the style of the translators’ supplied words (add), which is printed in roman and shown plain on the website, divides nothing among roman words, so that a compound it splits there is joined as any other. Hyphens may replace spaces between unchanged words, preserving each word’s styles and the matching note lemma. Five past tenses the King James Bible holds to, spake, begat, bare, brake, and sware, are carried through scripture as the inflections are. A compound takes the form current English gives it, closed, hyphenated as a modifier before its noun or wherever English keeps the hyphen, and otherwise open; the edition retains first-born, first-fruits, corner-stone, mercy-seat, stumbling-block, stumbling-stone, threshing-floor, ewe-lamb, turtle-dove, pre-eminence, battle-array, well-pleased, and money-changer, with their plurals, by explicit editorial preference. The named place nouns likewise take a hyphen, by editorial choice and not as a rule for every compound: burying-place, resting-place, dwelling-place, hiding-place, lurking-place, and market-place, with their plurals. Hiding-place and lurking-place need no decision: Brenton hyphenates them throughout (5 and 2, plurals included), and the King James Bible's open forms (4 and 2) stand only in books the edition takes from Brenton.

ligatures.why: The edition writes the ligatures out as their letters: æ as ae and œ as oe, in every word of the translations, their notes, and their front and back matter, names and Latin alike, so that no verse prints both spellings. It is done last, after every decision has been carried out and checked in the sources’ own letters, so the decisions name the forms the sources print; a decision that writes a word anew writes it with the letters.

names.why: Proper names of persons and places, respelled where their bearer is identified. A decision respells every whole-word occurrence of its forms in the verses it lists, as the edition numbers them, and in the lemmas that quote them, and nowhere else. Every other verse of the printed books that has a decided form is listed under keep, with who keeps it. The build refuses an occurrence listed neither way, a listed verse without its form, and a kept verse that another revision respells. Two bearers may share a source form, each listing its own verses, and where one verse names two bearers alike, each lists its occurrence by number, as LUK 6:16#1 and LUK 6:16#2. A note's commentary keeps the source's names, since the name there is often the note's subject. The front and back matter take the edition's names: a decision lists under matter the units that respell a form in every paragraph and footnote, and a decided form prints in the matter only where a decision lists it, so that the prefaces and Brenton's Introduction name the prophets and books as the edition does; the translators' and Brenton's other names, and their 1611 spellings of the Fathers, stand as they wrote them. The king of Judah retains both source names: Azarias for Greek Ἀζαρίας in 4 Kgdms and 1 Chr 3:12, and Ozias for Greek Ὀζίας, including 2 Chr. These names are not harmonized; other bearers and the related forms Azaria, Azariu, Ozia, and Ozi retain their source forms. A decision may also name the books whose terminal subscriptions respell a form under colophons; their wording otherwise remains the source’s. Subscription names must be met once in their named colophon.

Abijah, son of Jeroboam.why: Brenton's name for him where the Vatican text tells of his birth (3 Kgdms 12:24e), and the Greek's, Αβια; 3 Kgdms 14:1 is words the Alexandrine passage supplies from the King James Version (1KI 14:1-20).

Abraham, patriarch.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Matt 1:1).

Ahaz, king of Judah and other bearers.why: The king of Judah, the Benjamite of Jonathan’s line, and the father named at Jeremias 22:15. The King James Old Testament’s Ahaz, by which English readers know the king, in place of the Greek books’ Achaz (Matt 1:9), for recognizability, as Hosea; the other bearers take the same form, since the Greek name is one.

Ahijah the Shilonite, prophet.why: Brenton's name for him in the rest of 3 Kingdoms (11:29-30; 12:15; 12:24h-l), and the Greek's, Αχια; these verses are words the Alexandrine passage supplies from the King James Version (1KI 14:1-20).

Amon, king of Judah and father of Josias.why: The king of Judah, son of Manasses and father of Josias: Amon, the spelling of the King James New Testament (Matt 1:10), rendering the Greek Ἀμών. Brenton has Amon in Chronicles and Sophonias but Amos in 4 Kingdoms and Jeremias, where the Greek assimilates his name to the prophet’s; one Hebrew name underlies both, unlike Ἀζαρίας and Ὀζίας. The prophet Amos, the father of Esaias, and the ancestor of Christ keep Amos, as listed under keep.

keep.who: Amos the father of Esaias (4 Kgdms 19-20, 2 Chr 32, Esaias 1-38), the prophet Amos (Amos 1, 7-8; Tobit 2:6), and the ancestor of Christ (Luke 3:25).

Antioch in Syria.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Acts 6:5).

Aristeas, the narrator of the Septuagint.why: Brenton’s Introduction writes Aristeas three times and his Preface Aristæas once; the Introduction’s form, which is also the usual English one, serves both. Not the ligature written out, which would give Aristaeas.

Asher, son of Jacob and his tribe.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Luke 2:36).

Barak, Deborah's military leader.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Heb 11:32).

Beth-horon, upper and lower towns.why: The King James Greek books write the name both ways, Bethoron at Judith 4:4 and Bethhoron at 1 Macc 3:16, 24; 7:39; 9:50; Judith’s form serves every bearer, and the 1 Maccabees verses take it. The upper and lower towns name the same Beth-horon district in Joshua, Kingdoms and Chronicles.

Beth-shan, city.why: The Jordan-valley city, Bethsan in the King James 1 Macc 5:52 and 12:40–41 and already 3 Kingdoms 4:12.

Bethel, sanctuary, towns and mountains.why: The spelling of the King James Apocrypha (1 Macc 9:50), for Jacob's town and sanctuary, the town of the south (Jesus Navi 15:30) and the mountains of Song 2:9.

keep.who: Bæthel-berith (Judges 9:46, 50), a compound name.

Bethlehem in Judah and Zabulon.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Matt 2:1), for the town of Judah and for Abaissan's Bethleem (Judges 12:8, 10).

Boaz, husband of Ruth.why: Ruth’s husband. The King James Old Testament’s Boaz, by which English readers know him, in place of the Greek books’ Booz (Matt 1:5, Luke 3:32), for recognizability, as Hosea.

Caleb, son of Jephunneh, Esrom’s son, an.why: The faithful spy, son of Jephunne, called Caleb in the King James Sirach 46:7, 9 and 1 Macc 2:56 and already in Num 32:12, and Esrom’s son Caleb of 1 Chr 2:18–50, whom Swete writes Χαλέβ as he writes the spy and the Hebrew and the King James Old Testament write Caleb: a respelling of a name’s form reaches every bearer to whom the Greek and the Hebrew both give that name. The two men of Chronicles whose Hebrew names differ keep Brenton’s Chaleb, as listed under keep.

keep.who: Chelubai at 1 Chr 2:9 and Chelub at 1 Chr 4:11, whose Hebrew names differ from Caleb’s and whom the Greek alone wrote alike (Swete has Χαβέλ at 2:9); Brenton’s form stands.

Corinth, city.why: The city named Corinth in Acts 18:1, 1 Cor 1:2, 2 Cor 1:1, 23 and 2 Tim 4:20. The Romans subscription’s Latinized Corinthus names the same place.

Eber, ancestor of Abraham.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Luke 3:35). 1 Chr 1:18-19 are words the Alexandrine passage supplies (1CH 1:11-23).

keep.who: The sons of Edem in Thaesthen (4 Kgdms 19:12), a people.

Elijah, prophet.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Matt 11:14).

keep.who: Eliu the ancestor of Judith (Judith 8:1).

Elisha, prophet.why: The prophet. Elisseus stands nearer the Greek Ἐλισσαῖος of the New Testament and Alexandrinus, keeping its double consonant, than the King James Eliseus (Luke 4:27).

En-gedi, oasis.why: The oasis, called Engaddi in the King James Sirach 24:14 and already 1 Kingdoms 24:1; 2 Chr 20:2 identifies it as Asasan Thamar.

Ezekiel, prophet.why: The spelling of the King James Apocrypha (Sirach 49:8).

Gad, son of Jacob and his tribe.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Rev 7:5).

keep.who: Gaddi the spy of Manasse (Num 13:11) and the father of Manaem (4 Kgdms 15:14, 17).

Gennesaret, land and lake.why: The land named in Matt 14:34 and Mark 6:53 and the lake of Luke 5:1: RP2026 has Γεννησαρέτ in all three, and the King James Matthew and Luke write the doubled n for the same place.

Gideon, judge.why: The judge. The King James Old Testament’s Gideon, by which English readers know him, in place of the Greek books’ Gedeon (Heb 11:32), for recognizability, as Hosea.

Goliath, defeated by David.why: The spelling of the King James Apocrypha (Sirach 47:4).

Habakkuk, prophet.why: The prophet, including the superscription of his prayer (Abbacum 3:1).

Haggai, prophet.why: The spelling of the King James Apocrypha (1 Esd 6:1), including the Psalm superscriptions that name the prophet. The translators’ preface names the prophet Haggai once, and takes the edition’s name.

Ham, son of Noah and eponym of Egypt.why: Noah's son and Egypt named after him.

keep.who: Anna the wife of Tobit, and the prophetess (Luke 2:36).

Haran, city of Abraham.why: The city of Abraham, called Charran in Acts 7:2, 4 and already in Gen 27:43. Deson’s son at Gen 36:26, Hebrew Cheran, and the people of Amos 1:5, Hebrew Kir, bear other Hebrew names that the Greek translator alone wrote Χαρράν; Brenton’s form stands for them.

keep.who: Deson’s son (Gen 36:26), Hebrew Cheran, whom the Greek alone writes as the city.
The people of Amos 1:5, Hebrew Kir, whom the Greek alone writes as the city.

Hebron, Judean city, the Levite, and oth.why: The city, Hebron in the King James 1 Macc 5:65 and already in Joshua 10:3, and every other bearer of the name: Caath’s son and his Levitical clan, and Chebron in Marisa’s genealogy (1 Chr 2:42–43), with Brenton’s Chebrom at Gen 13:18 and 1 Chr 15:9. Swete writes them all Χεβρών and the Hebrew and the King James Old Testament write them all Hebron; a respelling of a name’s form reaches every bearer to whom the Greek and the Hebrew both give that name.

Hermonites, in Psalm 41's lament.why: The Ermonites of Psalm 41:7, a people, not the mountain.

Hezekiah and other bearers of Ezekias.why: The king of Judah, including the superscription of his prayer (Esaias 38:9) and Jeremias 33:18-19 and 2 Macc 15:22, which name him; and the other men named Ezekias: the ancestor of Ater's house, the ancestor of Sophonias, and the Ephraimite chief, son of Sellem. Hezekias stands nearer the Greek Ἑζεκίας, rendering its rough breathing, than the King James Ezekias (Matt 1:9).

Horeb, mountain of Moses.why: The spelling of the King James Apocrypha (Sirach 48:7).

Hosea, prophet and king of Israel.why: The prophet, and Osee son of Ela, king of Israel.

keep.who: Osee of Bæthsamys, in whose field the ark rested (1 Kgdms 6:14, 18), and the chief of the people who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:24).

Isaiah, prophet.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Matt 3:3). Brenton’s Introduction names the book Isaiah once, and the translators’ preface the prophet Esay once; both take the edition’s name.

Ishmael, son of Abraham and other bearer.why: Abraham's son, the son of Nathanias who slew Godolias, and every other Ismael.

Issachar, son of Jacob and his tribe.why: The tribe (Rev 7:7). The King James Old Testament’s and Brenton’s Issachar, which the King James text prints Isachar at Rev 7:7 alone; one form for the one name.

Jeduthun, temple musician.why: The spelling of the King James Apocrypha (1 Esd 1:15), for the temple musician and his Psalm superscriptions.

keep.who: Idithun of the genealogy (1 Chr 9:16) and the father of Abdedom the door-keeper (1 Chr 16:38).

Jephunneh, father of Caleb.why: The father of the faithful spy: the established King James Greek-book form at Sirach 46:7, Caleb the son of Jephunne. Both Brenton spellings name that same father.

Jeremiah, prophet.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Matt 16:14), for the prophet alone.

Jesse, father of David.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Matt 1:5). 1 Kgdms 17:12-20 and 17:58 are words the Alexandrine passages supply (1SA 17:12-31, 17:55-58).

Joash, father of Gideon and other bearer.why: Gideon's father, the kings of Judah and Israel, the king's son, and every other Joas.

Jonah, prophet.why: The prophet swallowed by the sea monster, already Jonas in the King James Greek books (Matt 12:39–41) and in Tobit 14:4, 8.

Jonas, father of Simon Peter.why: Peter’s father has the same Ἰωνᾶ in RP2026 and Scrivener at John 1:42 and 21:15–17; John 1:42 takes Jonas, the King James form of the three later verses, which is also how the King James Bible renders the prophet’s genitive Ἰωνᾶ (Matt 12:39). Matthew 16:17 retains the distinct compound Bar-jona.

keep.who: The son of Careth among the captains who came to Godolias; a different bearer, whom the King James Bible calls Johanan.

Joppa, port town.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Acts 9:36).

Joshua, son of Nun and successor of Mose.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Acts 7:45, Heb 4:8), for the son of Nun alone.

keep.who: The house of Jesue and Joab in the return (2 Esd 2:6).
Joshua the ruler of the city (4 Kgdms 23:8) and the father of Azur (Neh 3:19).

Josiah, king of Judah.why: The king, son of Amon, called Josias in Matt 1:10–11 and Sirach 49:1, 4 and already throughout the Kingdoms and Chronicles narratives; Swete declines his name, Ἰωσείας, and leaves it indeclinable at 1 Chr 3:14–15, which name the same king. The three men of 1 Chr 4:34, 11:46, and 25:15 bear other Hebrew names, Joshah, Joshaviah, and Jeshaiah, which the Greek alone wrote Ἰωσειά, undeclined; Brenton’s Josia stands for them.

keep.who: Amasia’s son (1 Chr 4:34), Jaribi’s son (11:46), and the temple musician’s house (25:15): Hebrew Joshah, Joshaviah, and Jeshaiah, whom the Greek alone writes like the king.

Jotham, king of Judah.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Matt 1:9).

Judah, son of Jacob, tribe, territory an.why: The patriarch; his tribe, territory, and kingdom; the Levite (Ezra 3:9); the official (Neh 11:9); the men of the dedication (Neh 12:34, 36); and the other ancestors named Juda. The Greek gives no help: the Received Text declines Ἰούδας for the men and writes the tribe Ἰούδα as its genitive, the Septuagint writes the patriarch and his tribe Ἰούδα undeclined beside Ἰούδας, and the King James Greek books write him Judas and Juda. Judah, the anglicized form of the King James Apocrypha at Sirach 49:4 and of its Old Testament, is taken for the patriarch and his tribe in both Testaments, as Abraham and Noah are, and chosen over Juda and Judas for recognizability, as Hosea and Gideon are, so that the patriarch and his tribe bear the name English readers know in both Testaments. 3 Kgdms 16:8 and 16:10 are words the Alexandrine readings supply.

keep.who: Judas the son of Calphi, a captain of Jonathan’s host (1 Macc 11:70), not Maccabaeus.
Judas Maccabaeus.
Simon’s son Judas, brother of John.
The Levite who put away his foreign wife, in the parallel returnee lists.
Judas Iscariot, Judas of Galilee, the host of Saul in Damascus, and Judas Barsabbas; at Luke 6:16 the second Judas of the verse, Iscariot, the first being the apostle Jude.

Judea, province.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Matt 2:1 and throughout), and Brenton’s own in 119 verses; he writes these three with the ligature.

Keilah, town of Judah.why: Brenton's name for the town in the rest of 1 Kingdoms 23 (23:1-13); 1 Kgdms 23:12 is words the Alexandrine passage supplies from the King James Version (1SA 23:12).

Kidron, brook east of Jerusalem.why: The Jerusalem brook called Cedron in John 18:1. The Kedron of Judges 1:30 is a town of Zabulon whose Hebrew name, Kitron, differs; the Greek translator alone wrote it Κεδρών, and Brenton’s form stands there.

keep.who: The town of Zabulon at Judges 1:30, Hebrew Kitron, which the Greek alone writes as the brook.

Luke, physician and companion of Paul.why: The same companion called Luke in Col 4:14 and 2 Tim 4:11, Greek Λουκᾶς in each passage. The subscription to 2 Corinthians names that companion too.

Mark, evangelist, companion of Peter and.why: The Evangelist. Μάρκος is one Greek name in every verse that has it, and the King James Bible writes it Mark in Acts 12 and 15 and at 2 Tim 4:11 but Marcus at Col 4:10, Philemon 24, and 1 Pet 5:13. This decision follows the identification of the three as one man in the Synaxarion for April 25, the feast of the Apostle and Evangelist Mark, which makes him the John Mark of Acts 12:12, the kinsman of Barnabas and companion of Paul of Col 4:10, and the son whom Peter greets from Babylon at 1 Pet 5:13, following Papias and Clement of Alexandria as Eusebius reports them (Ecclesiastical History 2.15, 3.39), who say that Mark wrote his Gospel from Peter’s preaching and that Peter means him by “Marcus my son.” He bears the name his Gospel bears throughout the New Testament, as Jude bears his epistle’s.

Megiddo, city and plain.why: The city and its plain, Magiddo in the King James 1 Esd 1:29, narrating the same battle of Josias as Brenton’s 1 Esd 1:27 and 2 Chr 35:22. Joshua and Judges name this same city in Manasses’s territory.

Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest.why: The king of Salem and priest. Melchisedek stands nearer the Greek Μελχισεδέκ, rendering its final kappa, than the King James Melchisedec (Heb 5:6), which keeps the Latin c, as Hezekias and Elisseus stand nearer their Greek.

Methuselah, son of Enoch and man of Cain.why: Enoch’s son, and the man of Cain’s line (Gen 4:18). The Greek Μαθουσάλα in the King James New Testament’s letters (Luke 3:37, Mathusala), with the final h that the King James Old Testament gives the Hebrew name (Methuselah), so that it reads in English as a man’s name and not a Greek feminine in -a; nearer the Greek than Methuselah, and nearer English use than Mathusala.

Micah of Moresheth and Micaiah son of Ga.why: The prophet, and Micaiah son of Gamarias.

Midian, patriarch, people and their terr.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Acts 7:29), for the patriarch, his people, and their territory.

Miletus, city in Asia Minor.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Acts 20:15).

Mordecai of Esther and the distinct retu.why: The King James Greek books’ Mardocheus: Esther’s hero is already so named at 2 Macc 15:36; the distinct returnee of Ezra 2:2 and Neh 7:7 is Mardocheus in the parallel 1 Esd 5:8.

Mount Hermon outside the dew passage.why: The spelling of the King James Apocrypha (Sirach 24:13), for the mountain.

keep.who: The dew of Aermon (Psalm 132:3).

Tabor, mountain, oak, and town.why: The mountain, Θαβώρ, where the Greek gives it that name; and the oak of Tabor (1 Kgdms 10:3, Θαβώρ) and the Levites’ town (1 Chr 6:62, Θαβώρ in Alexandrinus, whose reading Brenton followed), Hebrew Tabor as the mountain is, which the King James Old Testament writes Tabor too: a respelling of a name’s form reaches every bearer to whom the Greek and the Hebrew both give that name. The mountain’s other Greek name, Ἰταβύριον, is kept by its own decision.

Itabyrion, Mount Tabor under its other G.why: The mountain’s other Greek name, Ἰταβύριον in Swete at Hosea 5:1 and Jeremias 26:18, where the King James Old Testament, translating the Hebrew, has Tabor. Where the Greek gives one bearer two names, both are kept, as Azarias and Ozias are for the king of Judah; and one Greek name takes one English form, Brenton’s transliteration Itabyrion at Jeremias, in place of the Latin Itabyrium he wrote at Hosea.

Naaman, Syrian commander healed by Elish.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Luke 4:27).

Nadab, son of Jeroboam.why: Brenton's name for him where he reigns (3 Kgdms 15:25, 31), and Alexandrinus's at 14:20, Ναβατ (Swete, vol. I, p. 715); 3 Kgdms 14:20 is words the Alexandrine passage supplies from the King James Version (1KI 14:1-20).

keep.who: Nadab the son of Aaron (Exod 6:23; Lev 10:1; Num 3:2; 1 Chr 5:29).
Nadab the son of Samai (1 Chr 2:28, 30).
Nadab the son of the father of Gabaon (1 Chr 8:30; 9:36).

Nahum, prophet and ancestor of Christ.why: The spelling of the King James Apocrypha (2 Esd 1:40), for the prophet and the ancestor of Christ (Luke 3:25).

Nehemias, the governor, the son of Azabu.why: The spelling of the King James Apocrypha at 1 Esd 5:8 and 5:40, which Brenton has there too, and of this edition’s title for the book. Νεεμίας, Hebrew Nehemiah, names three men, so a respelling of the name’s form reaches them all: the governor, son of Chelcia (Neh 1:1, 7:70, 8:9, 10:1, 12:47, Neemia at 12:26; 2 Macc 1:18–36 and 2:13; Sir 49:13); Neemias son of Azabuch, who repaired the wall (Neh 3:16); and the returnee with Zorobabel (Ezra 2:2; Neemia at Neh 7:7). Brenton’s undeclined Neemia at Neh 7:7 and 12:26 is the same name.

Nineveh, Assyrian city.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Matt 12:41).

Noah, patriarch of the Flood.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Heb 11:7).

Nun, father of Joshua.why: The Orthodox spelling used in the edition's title Jesus, the Son of Navi, for Greek Ναυη (Ναυῆ, Ναυή, or Ναυὴ) at these places in Apostoliki Diakonia's text (https://apostoliki-diakonia.gr/holybible/). Numbers 13:8 and 13:16 correspond to its 13:9 and 13:17. Nun in 1 Chr 7:27 is retained: that text has the distinct form Νοὺμ.

Obadiah, prophet.why: The spelling of the King James Apocrypha (2 Esd 1:39).

Peleg, son of Eber.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Luke 3:35).

keep.who: Luke 3:35, which renders RP2026's Φαλέγ; its Textus Receptus note gives the King James Phalec for Φαλέκ.

Pharaoh, Egyptian royal title.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Acts 7:10).

Phinehas, son of Eleazar and other beare.why: Eleazar’s son, including the zeal recalled at 1 Macc 2:26, 54; Heli’s son; and the priestly ancestors and houses. Phineas is the English form of the Greek Φινεές, the Vulgate’s Phinees given an English ending, and keeps the Greek vowels and reads as a name, in place of the King James Old Testament’s Phinehas, which renders the Hebrew, and of the King James Greek books’ Phinees (1 Macc 2:26), a transliteration. The temple servants’ house at 1 Esd 5:31 is another name in the Greek, Φινόε, and keeps the source’s Phinees, as listed under keep.

keep.who: The temple servants' house at 1 Esd 5:31.

Phoenicia, coastal region.why: The region. The English name of the Greek Φοινίκη, in place of the King James Phenice and Phenicia (Acts 11:19, 15:3, 21:2), which English no longer uses for it, and of Brenton’s Phenice and Phœnice beside his Phœnicia. The haven of Crete at Acts 27:12, Φοῖνιξ, is Phoenix by its own decision.

Phoenix, Cretan haven.why: The haven of Crete at Acts 27:12. Phoenix is the English form of its Greek name Φοῖνιξ, in place of the King James Phenice, a form the King James Bible also gives the region Φοινίκη, which has its own decision.

Rahab, harlot of Jericho.why: The woman who sheltered the spies, Rahab in Heb 11:31 and Jas 2:25, Greek Ῥαάβ as in Joshua. Matthew 1:5 writes her Ῥαχάβ, and the King James Bible Rachab; two Greek spellings of one bearer are one name, as Ἀμών and Ἀμώς are Amon, and she is Rahab in Matthew too. The places Raab, the Syrian king’s father, and symbolic Egypt are other bearers, as listed under keep.

keep.who: The towns in Joshua 19:28; 21:31 and Judges 18:28, the father of Adraazar (2 Kingdoms 8:3, 12), and symbolic Egypt (Psalm 86:4).

Reuben, son of Jacob and tribe.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Rev 7:5).

Rhodes, island.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Acts 21:1).

Samaria, city and region.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Luke 17:11).

keep.who: Semeron the son of Issachar (1 Chr 7:1).
Mount Somoron (2 Chr 13:4).

Samson, judge.why: The spelling of the King James New Testament (Heb 11:32).

Sarah, wife of Abraham after the renamin.why: Abraham’s wife after her renaming at Gen 17:15. The King James Old Testament’s Sarah, by which English readers know her, in place of the Greek books’ Sara (Rom 4:19, Heb 11:11, 1 Pet 3:6), for recognizability, as Hosea; before the renaming she is Sara, as the Greek Σάρα distinguishes her from Σάρρα.

spoke.why: Five past tenses are carried through the text of Scripture and the lemmas and readings quoted in notes, as the inflections are: Brenton’s spoke, begot, bore, broke, and swore become spake, begat, bare, brake, and sware. The King James Bible holds to each without exception in the books of its canon and uses them constantly, spake 631 times and spoke never, begat 228, bare 208, sware 84, brake 77; its one begot and one forgot are participles, its two bore mean to pierce, and its swore and broke stand in the Apocrypha alone, twice and once, where the prevailing form is carried too. Prose keeps its author’s grammar, the participles stand, and so does bore where it means to pierce. The King James Bible is as constant in tare (4 times), forgat (9), trode (8), and ware (once as a past tense) but has them in a handful of verses, and these four are modernized wherever either Bible has them, as strake sail is: the choice is of which forms to carry, and the line is drawn where the counts leave a gap, between brake at 77 and forgat at 9. A verb the translators themselves used both forms of, drave and drove, gat and got, sang and sung, stands as each wrote it.

before-em-dash.why: An em dash supplies the break marked by an adjacent comma, colon, or semicolon. before-parenthesis.why: A parenthetical aside marks its own boundary. inside-parenthesis.why: A comma, colon, or semicolon inside a closing parenthesis belongs to the containing sentence: move it after the parenthesis, or remove it where an em dash follows and supplies the break.
